 US President Donald Trump has just delivered remarks to fellow world leaders in the Philippines, ahead of a dinner with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on the first day of his Asia tour.
 Here’s what else has happened the last few hours: 
 Trump arrived in Manila to an elaborate red carpet welcome , with a band blaring “YMCA” while troupes in traditional dress danced along.
 The president met with the leaders of India, Australia and Japan, an alliance known as the Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue .
 Speaking to reporters, he said Iran would pay a major price if it carried out an attack on Washington, after CNN reported yesterday that new US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC.
 He also said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un would like to join talks in China later this week.
 After this, Trump inked one of the main deals of his Asia trip, a trade pact with Thailand. While it is not a full trade agreement, Trump called it a “very big trade deal.” 
 CNN’s Kevin Liptak and Billy Stockwell contributed to this reporting.

 Trump signs trade papers with Thailand, but it stops short of full deal
 By Kevin Liptak in Manila
 Pool 
 President Donald Trump has inked one of the main deals of his Asia trip, a trade pact with Thailand.
 The agreement stops short of a full trade agreement, but Trump nonetheless just played up its importance in a signing ceremony with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
 Speaking to reporters, Charnvirakul cautioned that there was “still a little more to do.”
 “I’m confident that the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon,” he added.
 “It’s a joint statement agreement between United States of America, the Kingdom of Thailand, on reciprocal trade,” Trump then said when asked what, in fact, he was signing. “It’s a very big, actually, it’s a very big trade deal.”

 Trump says US will catch China on rare earths in 10 months. Data suggests it’s far behind
 By Logan Schiciano 
 US President Donald Trump speaks during a meeting in Manila on Tuesday. 
 Win McNamee/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump on Tuesday claimed that production of rare-earth minerals in the US will pull even with China within the next year, saying that the country is “making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before.”
 “We’re gonna catch (China) within 10 months,” Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with Quad leaders in the Philippines. “Everything that we need, we’ll have in 10 months.”
 CNN has reached out the Department of Interior for more information on Trump’s claim.
 As China has imposed export controls on rare earths in recent years, the US has ramped up production of these critical minerals – but data suggests the US is still well behind.
 In 2025, China produced 270,000 metric tons of rare earths and the US produced 50,000 metric tons, according to the US Geological Survey’s Mineral Commodity Summaries .
 China has historically dominated rare earth production. As of last year, China accounted for 61% of global mined rare earth production and its control over the processing stage was 92% of the global output, according to the International Energy Agency.
 The US possesses ample rare earths, but it processes an insignificant amount of them — the majority are refined in China. Processing rare earths is expensive, and US production facilities weren’t turning profits, and most have closed over the past couple decades.
 Some industry experts believe the United States could reduce its reliance on Chinese rare earths this decade through sustained investment in US processing capabilities. The Trump administration has announced billions of dollars in rare earth investments. But those facilities haven’t begun meaningful production to compete with China — and some aren’t expected to open until next decade.
 Rare earths are ubiquitous in everyday technologies and have been a major point of contention in the US-China trade relationship.
 China agreed to roll back certain restrictions on rare earth exports after Trump met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping Ping at last year’s APEC summit. The two men are set to meet again later this week.
 This post has been updated with additional information. CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

 Trump comments on report Deutsche Bank accidentally leaked tax statements
 By Kit Maher 
 President Donald Trump briefly commented on a report from the Financial Times that found Deutsche Bank accidentally leaked his tax statements in 2017.
 “Well, I paid a lot of tax,” Trump said, when asked about the report in Manila. “They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it.”
 The Financial Times reported that Deutsche Bank accidentally sent a client’s accountant year-end tax statements of 1,586 private bank accounts, including Trump’s. The accountant deleted the file and alerted Deutsche Bank, which described the incident as an “awful mistake,” the Financial Times reported, citing bank documents.
 CNN has reached out to Deutsche Bank for comment on the Financial Times reporting on Trump’s tax statements.
 In response to the overall investigation, Deutsche Bank responded, “The matters which are in focus of the media reports date back many years and in some cases as much as two decades. Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”
 “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation,” the bank added.
 Typically presidents voluntarily release their tax returns, but as a presidential candidate and during his first term, Trump said he wouldn’t release his taxes while under audit.
 Later in 2022, House Democrats released six years of Trump’s tax returns. CNN reported that he paid very little income tax at the time, claiming huge losses.

 Here's whats on Trump's schedule during his Asia trip
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 President Trump arrives in Manila, Philippines 
 US Pool 
 US President Donald Trump touched down in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, a short while ago, for the first leg of his trip to Asia this week.
 Here’s a look at what’s on his schedule during the visit:
 Tuesday
 Today, Trump is meeting with a number of world leaders, including the heads of state of Australia, India and Japan. These countries form the Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue , an informal group focused on security.
 Later, the president is expected to sign a trade deal with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
 Trump is also set to participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit, reception and dinner today.
 Wednesday
 Tomorrow, Trump is set to participate in a welcome ceremony with the President of the Philippines, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, as well as a bilateral meeting and a lunch.
 After this, he is expected to leave the Philippines and travel to Shenzhen , one of China’s most populous cities.
 Thursday
 Trump is expected to participate in a bilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
 Later in the day, he is also scheduled to take part in a trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
 We’ll make sure to bring you developments as we get them, stay with us.

 “It’s life,” Trump tries to send reassuring message after Chase Bank outage

 President Donald Trump assured that the software issue with Chase Bank, which caused thousands of people to have difficulty accessing their accounts, will be handled, downplaying concern about broader system outages in the United States.
 “It’s going to be very much under control,” Trump told reporters in Manila.
 When asked, the president said he’d spoken to the banks about it but did not specify to whom or elaborate on any of the conversations.
 CNN reported that it wasn’t a cyberattack, rather an update to Chase’s physical computer systems that was the root of the issue.
 Asked if he’s concerned about recent outages, including at Chase Bank, the FAA, Microsoft and United Airlines, Trump chalked it up to what happens in life.
 “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump said.
 Asked if he had any concern about Americans traveling for Thanksgiving, given the issues that caused Friday’s nationwide ground stop, Trump said: “No, not at all. People are safe.”

 By Billy Stockwell 
 US President Donald Trump speaks in Manila on Tuesday. 
 Win McNamee/Getty Images 
 US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un would like to join talks in China later this week.
 Asked if Kim was going to travel to China, Trump told reporters: “He would like to, yeah. We’ll see what happens.”
 On Monday, Trump said he “may meet” with Kim during his visit to China, adding that it would be up to Beijing’s leader Xi Jinping .
 Trump is traveling to Shenzhen, China later this week to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, where he plans to hold trilateral talks with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
 North Korea is not a member of APEC and Kim has not confirmed any plans to attend the summit. At a news briefing Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said he had no information on whether Kim would attend APEC this week.

 A closer look at the "Quad" of leaders set to meet with Trump later
 By Jessie Yeung 
 Travel pool 
 As we’ve reported , US President Donald Trump has landed in the Philippines, and will meet with the leaders of India, Australia and Japan. The alliance is known as the Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue .
 The partnership has its roots in the response to the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami, when the four countries set up a regional group to help relief efforts. But the Quad in its current form was created in 2007.
 It lasted barely a year due to a divergence of interests and pressure from Beijing , crumbling in 2008 when Australia announced its withdrawal from the grouping to pursue closer trade ties with China.
 But it was revived in 2017 amid renewed concerns about China’s rapid rise as a global superpower and Beijing’s increasingly aggressive foreign policy. The group then grew more active, with the heads of state meeting in person for the first time in 2021.
 Though sometimes dubbed by critics as an “Asian NATO,” the Quad is not a formal military alliance but an informal forum, featuring semi-regular summits, information exchanges and military drills.
 Quad members cooperate across fields including natural disasters, climate change and sustainability. But security and the goal of a “free and open Indo-Pacific” are key focuses, with the four nations frequently highlighting threats such as terrorism, disinformation and territorial disputes.
 The Quad has increasingly been seen as a counterweight to China’s growing reach in the region, with all four nations experiencing turbulent relations with Beijing in recent years.
 The strategic location of each of the Quad nations – at different corners of Asia-Pacific and with China between them – has rattled Beijing, which fears the potential for military encirclement. As recently as this May, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said of the Quad: “We are consistently against forming exclusive groupings and inciting bloc confrontation.”

 By Stephanie Yang 
 At their last meeting, President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping seemed ready to back away from confrontation amid an escalating tech rivalry, and even potentially collaborate on AI development safeguards.
 The Nvidia scandal could end all that.
 Days before Trump is set to meet Xi in Shenzhen, the US Commerce Department increased restrictions on exports of advanced US semiconductors in an effort to further limit China’s access to them.
 The measures announced Monday will apply to overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes” of computing power to a list of countries including China, and require new licenses for exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, due to a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion, or rerouting chips to unauthorized buyers.
 The rule change follows growing controversy over Nvidia, the world’s biggest supplier of advanced AI chips, and its sales to a Singapore-based company Megaspeed that is under investigation for potentially diverting server shipments to China.
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after reports he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US officials suspected of being part of an intelligence operation by China.
 Beijing has called the allegations groundless and an attempt to smear China. But the scandal has bolstered US efforts to strengthen tech export controls, which could derail recent efforts to ease trade tensions or even provoke retaliation from China.
 At a press briefing on Tuesday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing “will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
 Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the new restrictions were “a typical case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction. It runs counter to the consensus reached by both sides.”

 Why is Trump heading to the Philippines?
 By Kathleen Magramo and Helen Regan 
 US President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16 in Washington, DC. 
 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images 
 US President Donald Trump is the last leader expected to land in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit on Tuesday, two days after the event kicked off.
 Trump will attend the US-ASEAN Special Summit scheduled that evening local time, which a Filipino diplomat said would be “the last engagement to cap the meetings on 17 November.”
 So, why is Trump bothering to make an appearance at all? Well, his attendance underscores Washington’s desire to engage with the economic bloc as part of its efforts to counter growing Chinese influence in the Asia-Pacific region.
 ASEAN’s 11 member countries are a motley bunch. They include US allies Thailand and the Philippines, military-ruled Myanmar, communist-run Vietnam and Laos and economic giant – and the world’s most populous Muslim nation – Indonesia.
 Another member is the wealthy city-state of Singapore, currently under global spotlight over Megaspeed , a company based there that US officials suspect was at the center of a shadow industry of complex transactions and shell companies that facilitated chip smuggling to China.
 There’s plenty on ASEAN’s agenda at the Manila summit: from rising fuel prices sparked by the US and Israel’s war with Iran, to toxic smog in the region.
 Trump will meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr as well as the leaders of the other three so-called “Quad” countries: India, Japan and Australia. The Quad is an informal strategic forum focused on the region, featuring summits, information exchanges and military drills.

 President Donald Trump said Monday that he’s not considering replacing Commerce Secretary Howard Luntick, even as scrutiny intensifies over whether he should have done more to limit the sale of advanced chips to China.
 Trump downplayed reported disagreements between Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying that the two men “have two different views” over whether the Commerce Department should have moved faster in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat.

 Trump defended Lutnick’s decision to delay labeling Megaspeed a national security threat.
 “Well, he might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have, if you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow-up with China,” Trump told CNN’s Alayna Treene.
 “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it. And I’ll make a decision, but I understand very well both sides,” he added.
 In a tense Situation Room meeting earlier this month, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed.
